abstract: Agriculture faces several key challenges for meeting increasing demands for food, feed, and fuel while conserving natural resources and protecting the local and global environment.The advent of Smart Farming Innovations (SFIs) since the mid-1990s in the global North has the potential to simultaneously increase productivity by increasing the efficiency with which inputs are used and thereby reducing the loss of inputs to the environment which leads to damages to soil and water quality as well as to greenhouse gas emissions (1).These technologies enable site-specific crop management that is responsive to the substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity in soil conditions and variability in weather while also being less labor-intensive.Availability of these technologies is, however, not sufficient to ensure that this potential will be realized.Realization of the environmental benefits of SFIs will depend on the extent and mix of the suite of technologies adopted and the locations where they are adopted (2).Private incentives for adopting these technologies may need to be supplemented by policy driven incentives that are targeted to sources and regions where they can effectively mitigate the environmental disservices generated by agriculture.Empirical evidence about economic viability of SFIs has remained fragmented, often limited to individual technologies, crops, countries, or experimental settings (3).Roman et al. (4) apply an innovative methodology to provide the first globally explicit assessment of where SFIs are likely to be economically profitable, the role of environmental governance in accelerating adoption and the extent to which adoption will occur in locations that overlap with those facing major environmental challenges.Their study compiles a unique global database of 4,422 georeferenced observations of the adoption of five SFI technologies that include: mapping for precision agriculture, automated input application, Global Positioning System (GPS) steering assistance systems, autonomous weeding machines, and autonomous irrigation.The authors combine it with an ensemble of machine learning methods to map the potential for technology diffusion across global croplands based on macroeconomic drivers and project how this potential may evolve under future socioeconomic development pathways and environmental governance scenarios.The paper goes beyond the insights about the profitability of SFIs and the drivers of adoption obtained through isolated case studies and regional adoption surveys to provide a global perspective using a unified framework.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Realizing environmental benefits through the diffusion of smart farming innovations

abstract: Local atomic structures at ferroelectric domain walls (DWs) and anti-phase boundaries (AFBs) in HfO2 vary with the orientation and arrangement of neighboring domains, but the physical principles governing their formation remain unclear. Here, we establish a theoretical framework that predicts these local structures from the sign reversal of collective atomic displacement patterns across domain boundaries. We show that such reversals induce specific additional lattice distortions, which can be predicted from the symmetry relationships connecting the crystal’’s vibrational modes. Our approach demonstrates that differently oriented domain walls can exhibit identical local atomic structures, whereas other configurations develop distinct orthorhombic-like or monoclinic-like motifs. We further apply this framework to complex multidomain structures and Pbca antipolar phases, revealing that the compatibility of local shear distortions affects their structural stability. These findings establish a unified physical picture connecting domain boundaries, induced lattice distortions, and local atomic structures, providing a predictive approach to understanding complex interfaces and metastable phases in ferroelectric materials.
title: Phonon band connectivity-driven local motif formation at domain walls in HfO 2

abstract: When the length of an optical cavity is modulated, theory predicts exponential concentration of energy around particular space-time trajectories. Viewed stroboscopically, photons in such a driven cavity propagate as if in a curved spacetime, with black hole and white hole event horizons corresponding to unstable and stable fixed points of the evolution. Such phenomena have resisted direct experimental realization due to the challenges associated with achieving effective near-relativistic accelerations of massive cavity mirrors. We report results of an experiment that overcomes this limitation by exchanging the roles of light and matter. A matter wave endowed with quasirelativistic dispersion is confined between two barriers made of light, one of which is periodically translated at speeds comparable to the matter wave group velocity. In this strongly modulated cavity we observe the emergence of the predicted bright and dark fixed point trajectories, and we furthermore demonstrate that changing the modulation waveform can vary the number of fixed points and exchange their stability character. We observe signatures of nontrivial dynamics beyond those predicted for photons and attribute them to residual curvature in the dispersion relation. In addition to experimentally realizing and characterizing cavity dynamics in the ultrastrong driving regime, these results point the way to implementations of related dynamics in electro-optic materials, with potential applications in pulse generation and signal compression.
title: Matter-Wave Fabry-Pérot Cavity in the Ultrastrong Driving Regime

abstract: We formulate a time-dependent density functional theory for the coupled dynamics of electrons and nuclei that goes beyond the Born-Oppenheimer (BO) approximation. We prove that the time-dependent marginal nuclear probability density |χ([under [under R]_]_,t)|^{2}, the conditional electronic density n_{[under [under R]_]_}(r,t) and the current density J_{[under [under R]_]_}(r,t) are sufficient to uniquely determine the full time-evolving electron-nuclear wave function, and thus the dynamics of all observables. Moreover, we propose two time-dependent Kohn-Sham (KS) schemes which reproduce the exact conditional electronic density and current density and the exact N-body nuclear density. The remaining task is to look for functional approximations for the Kohn-Sham exchange-correlation scalar and vector potentials. Using a model driven proton transfer system, we numerically demonstrate that the adiabatic extension of a beyond-BO ground state functional captures the dominant nonadiabatic effects in the regime of slow driving.
title: Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory of Electrons and Quantum Nuclei

abstract: China is transforming its agricultural landscape by building 67 million hectares of high-standard farmland and is aiming to expand this area to 90 million hectares by 2030 (1). By improving irrigation, drainage, soils, and resilience to droughts and floods, the program has become central to China’s food security and climate adaptation. However, the rapid expansion overlooks the importance of clean agricultural drainage water. Before the completion of the planned farmland, China should ensure that the fields do not increase pollution in downstream waterbodies.
title: China’s farmland needs clean water drainage

abstract: On 9 September 2026, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) proposed narrowing the definition of “waters of the United States,” limiting federal wetland protection to those touching perennial water. This criterion reduces eligible wetlands even further than the 2023 Sackett v. EPA standard did (1, 2). After the Sackett decision, 19 to 91% of nontidal wetlands were at risk of losing protection, depending on interpretation (3). The EPA’s own regulatory analysis could not produce a reliable national estimate and relied on qualitative judgment instead (4), in part because its National Wetlands Inventory (NWI), which was partially built from decades-old aerial photography, was not designed for regulatory use (4). Obtaining more-accurate and up-to-date wetland maps is therefore essential before revisiting the US rules that define protected waters.
title: US water protection maps undercount wetlands

abstract: On 25 October 2013, Science published the Research Article “Mucus enhances gut homeostasis and oral tolerance by delivering immunoregulatory signals” by Meimei Shan et al. (1). Comments on PubPeer (2) identified duplications within figure S20G and between figures S20B and s20G that were validated by Science and confirmed by the authors. The experimental work related to this paper was concluded in 2013, and the source data are no longer available. Science is posting this Editor’s Note to alert readers to these issues. We are not taking further action because the main conclusions of the paper remain supported.
title: EDITOR’S NOTE on the Research Article “Mucus enhances gut homeostasis and oral tolerance by delivering immunoregulatory signals”
